summary: Observation of several red balls. Variable speed.
description: On the evening of November 19, 1982, a motorist and his passenger spotted luminous orbs in the sky. They were moving at varying speeds and were red in color. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On October 21, 1981, at approximately 6:45 PM, three witnesses saw a very bright, rapidly moving sphere for a few seconds. This sphere, initially white, had a trail and turned red before disappearing. This observation exhibits all the characteristics of an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Nighttime observations of a luminous orange saucer-shaped phenomenon low on the horizon: mistaken for the Moon near its rising.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named PALAISEAU (91) 1982, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On September 6, 1982, at 10:30 PM, a couple on their third-floor balcony spotted a large, orange-colored luminous phenomenon in the direction of the Orly runways. The witnesses compared the object to a saucer or an airship. The observation lasted two minutes, during which the phenomenon gradually disappeared. No noise was heard during the observation. The police investigation, involving various air traffic control services and local fire stations, yielded no further information. Of moderate strangeness and consistency (two dependent witnesses, no photograph), this case appears to have been a case of mistaken identity with the Moon near its rising (see the investigation report). The description of the UFO and the details of the police investigation strongly suggest a case of mistaken identity with the Moon: a large oval-shaped UFO, orange in color, bright light, leading to the hypothesis of a fire. The witnesses, despite having excellent visibility from their balcony to the east, stated that they did not see the Moon in the cloudless sky, even though it was clearly visible in the direction they indicated, at a low altitude that could explain its orange color. The fact that an aircraft passed between the UAP and the witnesses shows that the UAP was slightly to the right of the Orly airport runways, which perfectly corresponds to the Moon's position. The presence of clouds on the eastern horizon, not mentioned by the witnesses but deduced from meteorological data, explains (for T2) the UAP's disappearance by shrinking due to the progressive obscuring of a cloud, just as it explains (for T1) a departure towards the east, since T1 interprets the shrinking as a movement in distance, which is indeed towards the east. During the first investigation, GEIPAN did not have the same means to assess the presence of clouds and did not yet have this feedback on the illusions of movement that clouds can create in front of the Moon or a celestial body. The case is class A: observation of the Moon.

summary: Observation of a luminous mass with a change of direction
description: On September 4, 1982, witnesses observed, around 2:00 AM, a luminous mass that remained stationary above a factory. They described this mass as a sort of triangle with red and gold lights of varying intensity. This mass then moved slowly and silently, eventually disappearing towards the sea. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of the rectilinear and silent movement at 20m above the ground of an ovoid, metallic grey object reflecting the sun's rays with a sudden disappearance: observation of a Mylar-type metallized nylon balloon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named MONT-SAINT-AIGNAN (76) 06.08.1982 (but also known as ROUEN-SAPINS (76) 1982), is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. A witness at the corner of the CD43 and Rue des Mouettes in Mont-Saint-Aignan (76) observed, on August 6, 1982, at 8:05 PM, the silent movement of a metallic gray, ovoid object 20 meters above the ground. The sun occasionally reflected its rays. The witness saw a red geometric figure resembling an "eye" to the side. The witness turned upon seeing another witness already present, but when he looked back in the direction of the object, it had disappeared. The witness gave a statement to the gendarmerie on August 11 but was unable to provide a more accurate estimate of the distances. On August 12, the gendarmes went to the scene; no other witness statements were collected, and no trace of the object was found. The physical characteristics (metallic appearance reflecting sunlight, ovoid shape, presence of a decorative element) and dynamic characteristics (regular movement in the direction of the wind) are entirely consistent with the hypothesis of confusion with a metallized nylon balloon of the Mylar type (see the investigation report). Such balloons already existed in 1982 and were often circular or ovoid in shape, decorated with a decorative design that could be highly variable and was itself circular. It was a Friday evening during the summer, which is conducive to a festive or recreational event of this type. It is possible that such a decorative design is predominantly red and, observed from a distance illuminated by the setting sun, appears to the witness to have the appearance of a bright red eye. Although the witness's terminology is not very explicit on this point (e.g., "I specify that at one point I turned around to look at this person, and it was when I looked back in the direction of the object that it disappeared."), it is possible to assume that the UFO's disappearance occurred while the witness looked away to see the other person who was also observing the UFO. It is unknown how long the witness turned around; perhaps long enough for the witness to have missed the UFO in their field of vision or for it to have disappeared. The evidence is rather weak, with little information to definitively refute (the duration of the witness's turn is unknown) or confirm a hypothesis that, as it stands, is nevertheless sufficiently probable to be considered. During the initial observation and investigation, GEIPAN had little to no experience with misidentifications caused by Mylar balloons (see the website www.geipan.fr for cases recorded since then; search for cases using the keywords "Mylar" or "balloon"). GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable observation of a "Mylar" balloon.

summary: Observation of a point of light larger than a star
description: On July 5, 1982, at approximately 7:30 PM, a peculiar luminous phenomenon was observed by several witnesses. An orange, ovoid mass twinkled while a point of varying intensity appeared to rotate irregularly around it. This mass was much larger than a star. The phenomenon disappeared into a cloud formation. No further information was gathered about this event.

summary: Observation of a disc-shaped object moving very fast
description: On July 3, 1982, a witness spotted a shimmering orange ball, 20 cm in diameter, from his kitchen window. The weather was very stormy, and the ball was located in front of a cloud formation approaching the area. During the observation, which lasted over a minute, the ball maintained the same trajectory and moved rapidly. The phenomenon disappeared abruptly. No further information was gathered about this event.

summary: Observations of the slow passage of a luminous orange object with a trail: probable observations of atmospheric reentry
description: At 3:00 AM on June 16, 1982, witnesses observed a spherical object in the sky within a halo, followed by a series of smaller, yellow-orange dots forming a luminous trail. This array moved slowly in a straight line from the northeast to the southeast. The observation lasted less than a minute, and no noise associated with the phenomenon was heard. Based on their descriptions, these individuals likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Probable sighting of a balloon
description: On June 10, 1982, several people, including staff from an airport control tower, spotted a bright point in the sky. The investigation revealed that pilots also saw this bright object and that it was probably a stratospheric balloon launched by CNES from the Gap site, drifting and moving at an altitude of 30,000 to 40,000 meters, propelled by southwest winds after the release of its payload.

summary: Observation of the passage of bright points in the sky: lack of information.
description: Recent testimony (September 8, 2013) of an old observation, the date of which is not certain, as provided by the witness. The date of June 25th is given arbitrarily (taking into account some information provided by the witness). In late June 1982, several people gathered in the evening to watch the passage of a manned spacecraft in the starry sky. Around 3:00 AM, they were surprised to observe the passage of two other unknown luminous objects. Only one testimony was collected. The French First Manned Spaceflight mission took place from June 25th to July 2nd, 1982. The observation could have occurred on June 25th or 26th. The scenario described by the witness could be due to the coincidence of the apparent tracks of other satellites at different altitudes. The arrival of the third object could simply be its exit from the Earth's shadow, which allowed it to be suddenly illuminated by the sun. Orbital data for the multiple satellites in orbit at that time is unavailable. GEIPAN lacks the means to verify this hypothesis. This case is classified as Class C due to lack of information.

summary: Observation of a half-moon shaped object moving at variable speed and appearing to follow the witnesses: astronomical observations of the Moon.
description: This sighting was classified as a D case in 1982 by GEPAN. It was the subject of a new investigation (see document: Investigation Note). On May 16, 1982, at approximately 3:45 a.m., a driver and her passenger were intrigued by the presence of a luminous mass in the sky, described as a half-moon, orange in color. After remaining motionless above the town of Suippes, the UFO appeared to follow the witnesses, making horizontal hops, all the way to the village of Somme-Suippes. No noise was heard during the observation. The two witnesses lost sight of the UFO upon their arrival, as it was obscured by the landscape or buildings. No further information on this phenomenon was gathered by the gendarmerie. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, etc.) with a known astronomical phenomenon: the Moon at sunrise. Furthermore, the Moon was indeed present in the observed area of the sky, yet the witnesses made no mention of it, except to say that they initially thought of the Moon (which indicates that the UFO resembles our natural satellite). It is not the witnesses' visual perception that is at issue, but rather their interpretation of their observation through their feelings (fatigue and anxiety). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as UFO A: astronomical misidentification of the Moon.

summary: Observation of a reflective sign.
description: On May 10, 1982, a witness observed a peculiar flying object in the sky. For 45 seconds, he saw a rectangular panel that shimmered depending on its angle to the sun. Its north-south trajectory was constant. This object then disappeared into the landscape. Despite investigations, no further information (traces or eyewitness accounts) has been found regarding this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon illuminating the entire landscape and the silent passage of a round object: probable observation of an atmospheric reentry of a meteoroid.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named PONT SAINT-ESPRIT (30) 1982, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On April 28, 1982, at approximately 11:47 PM, a witness was startled by a flash illuminating the valley. He then observed a luminous phenomenon of a different color (green on the outside and white in the center). The entire object moved silently and very quickly at low altitude towards the west. The witness described a round object that remained unchanged in shape and color throughout the observation. No other witness accounts were collected. The testimony, left unexplained at the time, is re-examined 35 years later and appears consistent with numerous descriptions received since then by GEIPAN and identified as atmospheric re-entries of meteors or space debris. The characteristic features here are "a flash illuminating the valley" and "a very bright light, green on the outside and white in the center." It is common to have multiple witness accounts; nowadays, automatic cameras record and detect these re-entries. We cannot therefore guarantee this hypothesis, which nevertheless has a probability greater than 50% given the described appearance. We lack descriptive details regarding the duration of the event, which would help to determine whether it was a meteor or space debris re-entry. The lack of records for the second type leads us to consider the first type, which is the most frequently observed and the least well-documented (at that time). The strong glow in the sky illuminating the valley also supports this conclusion. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: observation of an atmospheric reentry of a meteoroid.

summary: Observation of 6 luminous orbs suddenly disappearing.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named CIOTAT (LA) (13) 21.04.1982, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On April 21, 1982, around 9:00 PM, a motorist spotted a formation of at least six luminous white V-shaped orbs above the La Ciotat golf course. For 15 seconds, he observed these orbs, which appeared stationary. No sound was heard. The formation disappeared instantly. No other witness accounts of this phenomenon have been collected. Despite the investigation by the gendarmerie, who at the time contacted the head of air traffic control at Salon-de-Provence, who confirmed that no aircraft from the Salon base were in flight at the time, all evidence points to the hypothesis of confusion with the Patrouille de France (and in particular their powerful nose lights, the only element visible over a long distance) flying in formation toward the witness for a few moments (see the investigation report). Perhaps this official wasn't the right person to determine whether or not the Patrouille de France was active (he didn't directly answer the question) or he wasn't authorized to share the information, even with the Gendarmerie. It is also documented that the Patrouille de France was in La Ciotat the day after the witness made their observation. The Patrouille de France (PAF), contacted and informed of the current evidence both supporting and refuting the hypothesis (air traffic control's opinion at the time of the observation), estimates the probability of the PAF's presence at that location and date at 60%, but no longer has the records to confirm this. Besides the above elements of plausibility regarding location and date, there are very strong similarities to this hypothesis regarding the Patrouille de France, in particular: - V-formation: there are at least three possible formations for the Patrouille de France that resemble a more or less elaborate V-formation; - number: presence of at least 6 spheres. The Patrouille de France aircraft can number a maximum of 8 or 9, but can also sometimes fly in smaller numbers; - color: white lights. The landing lights (or spotlights) are located on the nose of the Alphajets, which have been in service since 1981. The color is white or yellowish-white; - no perceptible noise: It is entirely possible that the aircraft were several tens of kilometers apart, and that the absence of perceptible noise is therefore hardly surprising; - trajectory: stationary UFOs. Observed moving towards the witness, they would indeed appear motionless for an observation period as short as 15 seconds; - duration: observation of approximately 15 seconds and instantaneous disappearance. The aircraft changed direction at the end of this period. Visible only by their nose lights, which have a limited beam angle, they became invisible to the naked eye due to the significant distance separating them from the witness. The elements of plausibility, reinforced by strong similarities, lead us to consider this hypothesis highly probable. The consistency is rather weak but nonetheless sufficient given the chosen hypothesis. Angular measurements are lacking, such as the size of the UFOs individually and collectively, and their altitude above the horizon. We do, however, have a drawing. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies this as A: highly probable sighting of a squadron of aircraft.

summary: Observation of a triangular-shaped object moving in a zig-zag pattern.
description: On April 21, 1982, around 11:00 PM, several CB radio operators spread across a large area called out to each other about a bright point of light. Through binoculars, this object appeared triangular, emitting an intense light. At a very high altitude, it zigzagged and sometimes hovered in place. No trail was seen behind the object. For some operators, the observation lasted until 3:30 AM before the object disappeared. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon, which remains unexplained.

summary: Long and multiple observations with the naked eye and binoculars of a very bright object that seemed to follow the witnesses in their movements: observation of the Moon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Among its publications are older cases, originally classified as type D, which are now being re-examined. The aim of this re-examination is not to lower or raise any particular classification category, but rather to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This case study, formerly known as GROIX (56) 13.04.1982, is one of the cases classified as type D by GEIPAN and has been recently revisited. On the island of Groix (Morbihan), during the night of April 13-14, 1982, at 2:45 a.m. (the most likely date of the sighting, according to the gendarmerie), three people observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky. Traveling in a vehicle to different locations on the island, the witnesses had the impression that the unidentified flying object (UFO) was following them or stopping as they did during their travels. One of the witnesses returned home and woke a fourth witness who confirmed the presence in the sky around 3:00 a.m. of a bright, stationary object that he did not recognize. The sighting continued in different locations on the island until 5:00 a.m. for some witnesses. The fourth witness made a similar observation the following day. The gendarmerie, alerted by chance on April 20, 1982, conducted an on-site investigation a few days later, but found no other witnesses. The investigation will not determine any EDF (French electricity company) disruptions, nor any particular observations from the Lann-Bihoué naval air base. The credibility of the witnesses is not questioned. The gendarmes indicate the phase of the Moon as last quarter. No traces on the ground or in the environment are found in the areas indicated by the witnesses. This case is moderately consistent: there are 4 witnesses, but with contradictions and inaccuracies (particularly regarding the date and the speed or direction of movement of the UFO). The described phenomenon presents many common characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, etc.) with observations of a well-known astronomical object: the Moon (see the investigation notes). The appearance of the UFO generally includes a semicircle, but the gendarmerie indicates in its investigation report that the Moon was in last quarter. T1 compares the UFO to a small planet that approached Earth. The UAP was observed over several hours (3 hours) and moved slowly across the sky, generally from west to east (despite some contradictions between witnesses)... similar to the Moon's movement. Furthermore, T4 reported seeing an object the following night in the same area of the sky with a shape identical to the previous one: the Moon was indeed visible again. The Moon was large (phase 0.7), clearly visible in the rather narrow area of the sky (east, southeast) described as the UAP's location, while the witnesses clearly stated they did not recognize the Moon: - if they claim not to have recognized it, it's because they also didn't see it next to the UAP; otherwise, at least two of them would have naturally said, "Besides, we could clearly see the Moon next to the UAP," to support the fact that it wasn't the Moon. Besides this, there is at least one who says, "It was pitch black, there was no moon." They couldn't possibly have missed it during such a long observation period, with a sky described elsewhere as clear and the moon's position at the end of the observation at 20 degrees of elevation above the ocean, in the direction of observation. This type of misinterpretation, generally caused by clouds or veils of clouds partially covering the moon, is frequent in the GEIPAN records (see the GEIPAN website with the keyword "Moon"). Here, in particular, we find the illusion of the following sphere (a perceptual illusion due to the witnesses' own movement), since the UFO seems to stop when the witnesses are stationary and resume its course when the witnesses move again. This perception generates strong emotions (perhaps even suggesting or hypothesizing the presence of an intelligence), and in doing so, can lead to a loss of precision in perception or memory. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: observation of the Moon.

summary: Observing an object moving slowly at a constant speed
description: Around 6:00 AM on April 12, 1982, several witnesses reported seeing a luminous phenomenon in the sky. Oval-shaped and orange in color, an object flew at a very high altitude but very slowly. Throughout the observation, which lasted approximately 10 minutes, the object did not change shape or color. Its speed remained constant. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Brief accounts of observations of the movement of a very bright round object in the sky: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as C and named THUMERIES (59) 04.04.1982, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation report). On April 4, 1982, around 10:30 PM, four people saw a luminous, round, white UFO in the sky. According to T1, the UFO was stationary above Thumeries, then moved north at very high speed. As it moved away towards Tourmignies (59), it left a red line in the sky that gradually faded (T2). The following elements: - T1: a luminous object, round in shape, white in color, very bright, - T1: stationary for approximately two minutes, - T1: three red dots below, - T2: It resembled a bright balloon. It seemed haloed. This could have been mistaken for a kind of fireball, and might suggest a helicopter; the absence of noise is not a valid argument since the distance is unknown and the wind is contrary to the propagation of sound towards the witnesses. The case is characterized above all by its lack of consistency. Indeed: - four witnesses observed the phenomenon, but only the testimonies of two of them have reached us. One witness failed to respond to the summons from the gendarmes; - these two testimonies are very brief and consist of only a few descriptive lines; - no thorough investigation by the gendarmes. No photographs were taken on site, nor was there a reconstruction, and no attempt was made to find other witnesses; etc. - numerous data points are missing, such as the angular elevations during the different phases of observation, the angular dimensions of the UFO, and the total duration of observation; - other data points are imprecise, such as the period of immobility of the UFO described by T1, as well as the manner in which it disappeared. The direction of movement of the UFO is also unclear (northward for T1, northeastward for T2); - finally, some data points are mentioned by one witness but not the other, such as the presence of three red dots under the UFO, mentioned only by T1. The sighting itself is not unusual, as nothing is inconsistent with the observation of a helicopter, but the overall evidence lacks sufficient consistency to support this hypothesis, even though nothing can disprove it. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of the probable re-entry of an object, either natural (meteorite) or of human origin (part of a craft)
description: On April 3, 1982, several people observed a luminous colored phenomenon that moved very slowly along a North-South axis. According to the director of the volcanological observatory, this phenomenon was probably due to the atmospheric reentry of a natural object (meteorite) or one of human origin (part of a craft).

summary: Observation of several groups of objects moving at very high speed
description: On March 30, 1982, several motorists observed cigar-shaped objects between 9:00 PM and 10:15 PM. These objects moved horizontally without making any noise. The colored objects moved in groups, and some at very high speeds. The available information did not allow for an analysis of the phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a glimmer. Object changing position
description: On March 12, 1982, at approximately 6:30 a.m., a witness observed a very bright light in the sky. Through binoculars, he saw an irregularly shaped sphere studded with points of light; during observation, the object changed position and color. No further information could be gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a luminous sphere. Probably atmospheric reentry.
description: On March 12, 1982, at approximately 8:30 PM, a witness observed a very bright, silvery-colored sphere in the sky, about 80 cm in diameter, followed by a light orange trail. Throughout the observation, the object did not change color or direction. This person likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Long, discontinuous observation of colored luminous balls in the night: lack of reliable information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D, is part of a set of recently re-examined cases. On the evening of February 27, 1982, at 8:15 p.m., a witness was watching television when he suddenly saw a luminous phenomenon through his living room window, described as a large ball and orange flames. Twenty minutes later, the witness observed, through the same window, three spheres one meter above the ground, emitting lights of different colors (red, green, orange). No sound was emitted by this phenomenon. The witness observed these objects until 10:45 PM. He watched television again and did not see the phenomenon disappear. Only one witness statement was collected. The witness remains shocked by his observation. This statement is characterized by a strong sense of strangeness because there is no solid hypothesis that could explain the appearance and presence for several hours of three or four luminous spheres, even though there are stranger phenomena than simple, fixed lights. It is also characterized by a lack of consistency in terms of information: the police took photographs on site to document the observed positions of the UFOs. The absence of measurements of the spheres' angular size and any details regarding their movement is regrettable. Most importantly, the witness made no observation of the disappearance of the phenomenon(es), and even more so in terms of reliability; - There is a significant inconsistency in the witness's account of the strangeness they experienced. The witness took 20 minutes to go to the window after being alerted by a luminous ball in the sky (with orange flames). After noticing three flashing balls one meter above the ground, the witness stated that they continued to observe the objects for 2.5 hours but did not see them disappear "because they were watching television." It is possible that the symptoms experienced following this observation (and which the witness associated with it) may have amplified a sense of strangeness (which was perceived as much weaker at the time of the observation), perhaps even influencing their memory or account. - The reliability of the information is flawed in several respects: the witness no longer mentions the initial light in the sky he observed from the window, whereas the police specify that it remained above the other three lights the entire time. The witness states that he has "never been interested in studying this type of phenomenon, either through reading or any other media," yet, in addition to knowing he can contact GEPAN (the French UFO research center) in less than a few business hours (Monday morning for an observation on Saturday evening) during a period without internet access, he claims the opposite to the police, adding that he has always wanted to be present at the time of a UFO sighting. The consistency of this testimony and all the other evidence collected is insufficient in absolute terms, especially considering the resulting strangeness. It is not possible to describe such an observation as unexplained or inexplicable, and therefore unusable. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of the slow movement of a large ball: lack of information.
description: On February 21, 1982, at approximately 6:15 a.m., two witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky. A bright red point was moving slowly southward. The same observation had been made in January 1981 and 1982 by another witness. The description suggests an astronomical observation, a hypothesis that cannot be verified due to a lack of evidence.

summary: Observation of 2 luminous objects.
description: On February 19, 1982, at approximately 6:30 PM, two witnesses observed a very bright, stationary point of light much larger than the evening star. Near this point, a cylindrical object was also stationary. It appeared to emit a cold, dull light. No noise was heard during the observation, which lasted about four minutes. As the witnesses moved, the objects disappeared into the landscape. No further information was gathered.

summary: Observation of a hexagonal object. No noise
description: On February 15, 1982, at approximately 7:00 a.m., witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon approaching the sky. One witness noted that flashing white lights emanated from each edge of a dark, hexagonal mass. No sound was heard during the object's movement. No further information was gathered about the observed phenomenon.

summary: Observation of an ovoid object moving in a back-and-forth motion from top to bottom.
description: On February 9, 1982, several witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon around 6:40 a.m. Ovoid in shape, it emitted a reddish-orange light. During the 47 minutes of observation, this object moved back and forth, from top to bottom. One of the witnesses stated that he had already observed this phenomenon during January and February at the same time. The witnesses' descriptions and the repeated observation over several days at the same time suggest an astronomical observation, although this hypothesis cannot be confirmed due to a lack of evidence.

summary: Observation of about fifteen objects with an elongated shape
description: On February 1, 1982, between 11:20 PM and 11:30 PM, several amateur astronomers observed about fifteen objects with binoculars. These objects were moving silently in a south-southeast direction. Slightly elongated and colored, they were very bright. No changes in shape or color were noticed during the observation. The available information does not allow for an analysis of the phenomenon.

summary: Observations of the silent movement of an illuminated flying object: astronomical mistake with the Moon.
description: On January 27, 1982, at approximately 7:15 PM, a family traveling in a car on the CD 910, in the town of Guenviller (57), observed a peculiar object in the cloudy sky for two minutes. It emitted a light and moved slowly and silently. It was shaped like a hemisphere. Two of the witnesses returned to the scene around 7:30 PM, but the object had disappeared. On the map (see map), the witnesses' route is shown as a black dotted line, and the direction of observation is shown in blue. The direction of observation was generally along the axis of the road, slightly to the left or right, depending on the phase of the observation, resulting in an azimuth between 242 and 244 degrees. An astronomical observation indicates (for Nancy, at 7:15 PM) that the Moon was at an azimuth of 244°, at an elevation of 4.5° (see celestial chart), and appeared as a thin, tilted crescent. Since the witnesses did not mention the Moon in their observation, even though it was directly in their field of vision, it was indeed the Moon they observed, misled by its low elevation and by some low clouds that partially obscured it, giving it a cigar or hemisphere shape. Aside from estimates of the object's size, the witnesses' account supports this hypothesis: a tilted, plate-like shape that moved from the right to the left side of the road depending on the vehicle's speed and direction, and stopped when the vehicle stopped. The object's disappearance corresponds to the gradual setting of the Moon and/or a passing cloud. This case, after having been class "D", is class "A": observation of the Moon at its setting.

summary: Long observations of a very bright orange object due east at low altitude: probable observations of the Blood Moon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named CHARLEVILLE-MEZIERES (08) 1982, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 17, 1982, at 1:30 a.m., two witnesses observed for a long time from their homes a luminous orange ball on the ground in a field, illuminating the surrounding area. The phenomenon was described as rising from the ground, leaving behind a kind of colored gaseous layer. The following day, the witnesses went to the presumed location of the UFO, but no trace was found on the frozen, snow-covered ground. The details reported in the official report are imprecise, and it is not possible 35 years later to contact the witnesses to expand upon or clarify these details. Nevertheless, with the experience acquired since then by GEIPAN (the French National Center for Information and Experimentation on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena), certain characteristic elements allow us to formulate a very probable hypothesis for this observation, namely that it was a lunar sighting. - The UFO remained stationary for a fairly long period (here, on the order of 15 minutes). - The described shape: "An enormous orange ball, with an intense light." - The Moon was indeed in the direction observed by the witnesses, and they did not notice it. We don't have the witness's exact address, but he indicates that his window faces due east and the Moon was indeed visible at 1:30 a.m. at an azimuth of 102° (almost due east) and at a low altitude (2.3°), which usually gives it a reddish or orange color. The low altitude might lead the witness to believe that "this orb was in the fields about 300 meters away, on a hill. The light was so intense that I couldn't see what was around it. This light illuminated the whole cluster of houses. To me, this orb was on the ground." The other witness, T2, says something more consistent with a UFO that was on the horizon and not against a landscape background (the doubt being justified by T1's statements): "I saw an object rising from the ground. I didn't see the shape, but I noticed something like a grayish-white gaseous layer with an orange color in the center that gradually diminished. The gray color became dominant. After this phenomenon, the object disappeared. We went to bed." The starting point of the misunderstanding is the failure to recognize the Moon. This most often stems from the presence of clouds or haze that partially obscure the Moon; T2's statements above ("something like a grayish-white gaseous layer with an orange color in the center that gradually diminished") indicate that this is very likely what it was. The cloud cover can reveal the Moon (variably or not during observation) with an outline of any shape (for T1, "as it moved away, I noticed it resembled what is called a flying saucer") or with a blurred or no outline when the cloud covers but does not block the light (for T1, "Once the object had left, a sort of orange vapor remained on the ground for a few minutes"). Many witnesses report a final movement of the UFO, sometimes very rapid. This is the illusion of receding into the distance. The reduction in the Moon's intensity due to increased cloud cover is "logically" interpreted by the witness as the UFO receding into the distance (which would have a constant intrinsic light intensity), especially since very often, as the gap in the clouds over the Moon closes, the angular size of the UFO decreases. Here, T1 does not explicitly give an indication of angular movement in The sky, T1 says, "She left in the direction of Sedan." However, around 1:45 AM (the observation time is not indicated, but we can assume that by the time T2 got out of bed and this strange phenomenon was minimally observed, 15 minutes had elapsed), the Moon was at an azimuth of 105°, and the direction of Sedan was centered around 128°. It is quite plausible that the witness described the flight in terms of distance (in the direction of the Moon) by approximating it with the direction of Sedan, unless the witness didn't know the direction of Sedan perfectly (to within 20°, which isn't a big error) or the witness had nothing more precise to indicate the direction of the Moon to the police (conveniently). The only geographical landmark in this direction seems to be the village of Fleigneux, which is as far from Sedan as the location itself. Furthermore, T2 does not indicate any final direction of movement. Note also that over 15 minutes the Moon rose 3 degrees in altitude, which is consistent with T2's statement, if the latter observed for a sufficient duration ("I saw an object rising from the ground") and 3 degrees to the right, which may have given T1 the idea of moving towards Sedan, assuming also that the observation period was sufficient and that T1 distinguished between the direction of the UFO and that of Sedan (the most likely scenario being that T1 associated the direction of the UFO with that of Sedan due to ignorance or convenience of reference). Given all the preceding elements, the hypothesis to retain is that of the Moon. It is not possible to state this definitively because, lacking the exact address of the witnesses, we cannot confirm the absence of a physical obstacle between the position of the witnesses and that of the Moon (although, in terms of general topography, beyond the first 100 meters). (unverifiable meters, no obstacles to the terrain present). Similarly, although the report indicates clear skies, it is not possible (no weather data available) to guarantee the absence of total cloud cover in front of the Moon. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable observation of the Blood Moon.

summary: Observations of a moving luminous phenomenon illuminating large areas of landscape over a significant distance: unexplained phenomenon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case study, previously classified as D and named ORLEANS (45) 1982, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 23, 1982, between 4:35 and 4:55 a.m., gendarmes from the highway patrol unit, on patrol on the A10 motorway (Paris-bound), spotted an undefined bright mass in the sky and a brightly lit area on the ground. Throughout their approximately 30-kilometer journey, they continued their observations, sometimes while driving, sometimes while stopped. No unusual noises were heard, particularly when the patrol was stopped. Several times they lost sight of the phenomenon before seeing it again. Toward the end of their observation, the bright mass was no longer visible, but the witnesses noted that the glow persisted to the east in some bushes bordering the motorway. An on-site investigation was conducted by the gendarmes, who contacted BA123 Orléans Air Base, located 7 km as the crow flies from the motorway: no planes or helicopters were in flight, and the base's radar station had been out of service since the previous evening. Cofiroute, the company that manages the A10 motorway, was contacted: no employee of this company had noticed the phenomenon. No other testimonies from residents living along the A10 were collected. A resident of Ingré (45), who witnessed a phenomenon on January 17, 1982, made a statement to the local press on January 19, 1982, a few days before the two gendarmes' observation, but never went to the police station to which she was assigned. The local press commented on the event in an article on January 27, 1982, linking the three testimonies. We explored two hypotheses that could explain certain physical or dynamic characteristics of the UFO (see the investigation report). It is established that the phenomenon was moving, not static, since it illuminated various parts of the relatively nearby landscape (pylons, hangars) over a significant distance. We know that celestial bodies (here, the planets Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars were present) can create perceptions of luminous phenomena following the witness when the latter is themselves moving. But we do not see how one of these celestial bodies could be perceived as a bright mass even through a cloud, and produce such focused ground illuminations. The hypothesis of confusion with a helicopter equipped with a powerful searchlight, located in or above the cloud layer, is more interesting. It would explain the unique perception of a bright mass, without a well-defined outline, and the absence of any perception of navigation lights. as well as the luminous phenomenon observed on the ground, illuminating various parts of the landscape, much like a helicopter spotlight would sweep across the area as it travels along the highway. Since spotlights are not designed to penetrate clouds, it must be assumed that the ground search mission with spotlights primarily operates through breaks in the cloud cover. This is not incompatible with the presence of a cloud obstacle between the witnesses and the helicopter, as the low cloud cover was not continuous (3/8 octas). The absence of perceived noise and a visible beam are not conclusive arguments. Depending on the meteorological conditions (wind speed and direction, air quality), noise may not be perceived, and a beam of light may not form if the air is clear. The relatively uniform cloud layer (3/8 and 6/8 octas on two levels) was located (barring any meteorological errors) at altitudes (1200 and 1500 m) placing the helicopter too far from the ground for the range of searchlights such as those equipping civilian and military helicopters of the time. Furthermore, the rather small portion of the illuminated pylon indicates that the object illuminating it, if located at cloud level, must have produced a highly focused beam, somewhat like a laser, which was also beyond the capabilities of onboard equipment at the time. The description, particularly by T1, of the landscape being illuminated by a phenomenon reminiscent of that produced by black light does not correspond to the hypothesis. Light used for research, for example, must, on the contrary, be bright, powerful, and clearly illuminate the entire surrounding landscape. Finally, why would the helicopter be flying above the clouds for a surveillance mission with a searchlight (through breaks in the clouds)? The hypothesis of returning from a mission with the searchlight left on is further contradicted by the fact that T1 had time to see the details of the pylon and perceived the lights to be stationary. The probability of such a hypothesis is too low to be considered. Moreover, the consistency appears sufficient to support an unexplained nature in its current state. In the current GEIPAN methodology, the present level of strangeness and consistency necessitates conducting a field investigation with the witness for a reconstruction and a cognitive interview. This latter process is likely to positively and negatively impact the assessment of both strangeness and consistency. However, it is not feasible for a case revisited so long after the event. Therefore, the evaluation of this case is conducted according to the current criteria for considering strangeness and consistency*, as if the field investigation had been carried out and had been completely neutral (no additional or missing information), which is sometimes the case. However, to highlight this methodological difference, the classification is based on ABCD and not on the current ABC D1/D2 classification, which, for the unexplained category, corresponds to a stronger validation of the unexplained nature of the case. Here, the case is on the borderline between an unexplained case and a case that cannot be investigated due to a lack of consistency in the case file, resulting from the absence of an on-site GEIPAN investigation. Consequently, the case is classified as D: unexplained. *(see The classification methodology at GEIPAN).

summary: Observation of a colored light phenomenon following a motorist on his morning journey: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case study, previously classified as D and named MARTIGUES (13) 1982, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 14, 1982, at approximately 6:40 a.m., a motorist on the Martigues road near Saint-Mitre-Les-Remparts (13) was intrigued by a colored light phenomenon that seemed to follow him as he moved and to remain stationary when he stopped. No sound was heard. Only one witness statement was recorded at the gendarmerie. This statement, as reported in the gendarmerie's official report, presents some characteristics typical of a UFO sighting. These characteristics are now well-known to GEIPAN (the French group investigating UFOs) due to the accumulation of explained cases of this type, particularly over the last ten years (see the website www.geipan.fr and search for cases related to celestial phenomena such as Venus, the Moon, and the Sun). The typical aspect here is the perception of being followed by the UFO: - The UFO's position is stable when the witness is stopped and becomes mobile as soon as the witness moves. The direction of the celestial body is, of course, absolutely fixed. When the car follows a roughly constant heading, the celestial body is stationary relative to the vehicle and moves past the landscape. Since the witness has already been surprised by the appearance of the UFO and considers it to be at a close distance, this movement along the landscape is interpreted as the UFO moving parallel to the vehicle, reproducing the vehicle's speed, here to the left of the witness on the road. If the car changes course, the direction of the celestial body changes relative to the reference point linked to the vehicle and the road, potentially causing the UFO to cross the road (as is the case here). The starting point for misinterpreting the following UFO is the failure to recognize the celestial body. This is quite common with bright stars at low elevations; atmospheric thickness alters the colors, creates scintillations (or, in this case, "flickering lights"), and perceptions of bursts of light, even slightly moving ones. Observing through a window or windshield also creates bursts of light into several points of brightness and/or colors, regardless of the star's elevation. On the morning of the observation, several celestial bodies could have contributed to the misinterpretation, some at low elevations (Capella 12th at an azimuth of 323°) and others at higher elevations (Jupiter 32nd at an azimuth of 165°, Vega 32nd at an azimuth of 6°). The hypothesis is plausible but cannot be confirmed because the other characteristic of the observation is its lack of precision. The elevation and azimuth of the UFO are not indicated, nor even the precise location and direction of travel of the witness. If the witness is traveling near Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts towards Istres, therefore on a heading oscillating between 285° and 360° (depending on their exact position on the road), Capella is a possibility, as they did indeed cross the road from left to right several times, reaching as far as 40° to the left of the vehicle's axis. If the witness is traveling in the other direction towards Martigues (more plausible since they live in Istres and travel to work), the heading oscillates between 180° and 105°. Jupiter, on a heading of 165°, could indeed cross the road, reaching as far as 15° to the left of the vehicle's axis. The description "very low on my left" in the witness statement seems a bit too vague to correspond to either of the above situations, especially the second one, which nevertheless corresponds to the most plausible direction of travel. However, the witness was not subjected to a standard police or GEIPAN questionnaire (only 10 lines of free-form information were provided by the police) to clarify positions and directions; it is possible that the witness may have taken a different route than the presumed main one. The statement is not precise enough to confirm or refute the celestial body hypothesis. In any case, it is somewhat unusual, given that, alongside the celestial body hypothesis, there is also the possibility of a helicopter. Being sufficiently distant, the helicopter could be unrecognizable and inaudible, and could also create the perception of a tracking sphere as the witness moved. The short duration of the observation makes this hypothesis possible, and the testimony neither confirms nor refutes it. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Brief and successive observations of a very strong, motionless and silent white glow; presence of a halo: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Its publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This case, previously classified as D and formerly known as MARTIGUES (13) 1982, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 12, 1982, between 5:45 and 6:15 a.m., two witnesses saw a very bright light through the half-open shutters of their room. The object is described as a luminous white sphere with a green halo that remains motionless and silent. Each appearance lasts a few seconds. The testimony of a third witness, reported by T2, indicates an observation made around 7:00 AM. The direct witnesses (who signed a police report) observed the sighting from their beds through the half-open shutters of their rooms. Their observations concerned a fleeting, fixed glow seen several times, for a few seconds each time, between 5:45 AM and 6:00 AM. The police report indicates that the bedroom window overlooks the highway bridge to the northwest and is 150 meters from the observation point. T2 places the UFO "at a height of 60 meters, near the highway bridge. The bridge itself is 45 meters high." These elements indicate a low-elevation UFO in a northwest direction. The UFO's height was estimated at 60m - 25m (the height of the 8th floor), observed at 150m, or around 12° elevation. One hypothesis could be the observation of Capella. This star moves towards an azimuth of 320° and a site of 15°, placing it in the Northwest sector. Due to atmospheric turbulence at low elevations, Capella can appear with varying colors consistent with those observed (white and green). T1 indicates that it was raining. The sky may not have been completely overcast, allowing Capella to appear fleetingly. The passage of cloud cover can alter the star's intensity and give the impression of proximity to or distance from the observers. The witnesses nevertheless reported a very bright light for a Capella sighting: T1: "very intense. I thought it was a thunderstorm or a factory flash." T2: "the central point was very brightly lit," "a light that encompassed the entire neighborhood." In fact, they made the observation from their beds through the partially open shutters (T1 indicated not having moved from bed, and T2 having observed before getting up; there was no longer a UFO during the subsequent observation from the balcony). This observational condition may have accentuated the impression of surprise and the intensity of the light. But this same observational condition seems to indicate a restricted angular field of view around the building's normal, which reduces the probability of the Capella hypothesis, without, however, ruling it out (as shown in the attached reconstruction). Another hypothesis would be ball lightning. The rainy weather, the colors and the halo, and the short duration suggest this type of phenomenon, which can appear during a stormy atmosphere (yellow + pale green halo). See the article Aspects, manifestations and classification of ball lightning. This would explain more directly (than the Capella hypothesis) the perception of a strong flash and also of a ball or halo (although these latter perceptions sometimes also accompany observations of celestial bodies). We do not have the statement of the third witness reported by T2, but only what was recorded in the official report. Between 7:00 and 7:15 AM, he saw a flash in the shape of a bluish-white hemisphere. This very strong and silent flash lasted two seconds. The observation seems incompatible with Capella due to the direction (see reconstruction), but it is consistent with ball lightning. This last event can occur fleetingly during stormy weather, even up to an hour (7 AM) later than the observations of T1 and T2. The observation is not very strange, as the glow could result from a star or, more likely, from ball lightning. The very poor observing conditions, particularly the limited field of view (from the bed through the partially open shutters), did not allow for a proper observation of the appearance, evolution, and disappearance of the UFO—elements crucial for further investigation and confirmation of one of the hypotheses (especially regarding ball lightning). The third testimony also lacks consistency (precision, reliability) due to its indirect nature. In conclusion, these are relatively strange accounts, possibly corresponding to a star or, more likely, to a ball lightning event, but which cannot be properly analyzed due to their limited consistency. GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information. Observations made on other days, reported by T2 and recorded in the report, are unusable (lack of information, no precise date).

summary: Likely sighting of a civilian airliner with its "sparkler" navigation lights
description: On January 6, 1982, in the late afternoon, witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon. An object emitting red, white, and blue lights moved slowly and disappeared over the horizon. The investigation revealed that a civilian airliner with "flashing" navigation lights of the same colors had passed overhead between 6:00 and 7:00 PM.
